title: Pseudo-Augustini Quaestiones Veteris et Novi Testamenti CXXVII
author: Ambrosiaster
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0022a.stoa001.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Et si tempus promissionis requirant, sicut Danihelo profetae ostensum est, inuenient inpletum tempore quo natus et passus est Christus, quia a tempore primi anni Darii regis Persarum usque ad natiuitatem et passionem domini et excidium Hierusalem, quod factum est per Uespasianum imperii Romani principem, inpletae sunt ebdomadae LXX, qui sunt anni CCCCXC. qui conputus per regna et per successores imperii manifestus est, quo modo etiam a Tertulliano conputatum inuenitur in Iibro, quem scripsit aduersus Iudaeos, quod ne ad iniuriam eius proficeret, quia recte conputauit, praetermisimus.
passages.english: And if they ask for the time of the promise, as it was shown to the prophet Daniel, they will find it fulfilled at the time when Christ was born and suffered, because from the time of the first year of Darius, king of the Persians, up to the birth and passion of the Lord and the destruction of Jerusalem, which was carried out by Vespasian, emperor of the Roman empire, the seventy weeks were fulfilled, which are four hundred and ninety years. This reckoning is clear from the reigns and from the successors of the empire, as it is also found reckoned by Tertullian in the book which he wrote against the Jews; we have passed over this, so that it should not tend to do him an injury, since he reckoned correctly.
passages.notes: 'Iibro' is a scanning error for 'libro' (book). The final clause ('quod ne ad iniuriam eius proficeret... praetermisimus') is obscure: the sense seems to be that the author omits repeating Tertullian's calculation so as not to slight or diminish him, since his reckoning was correct; the referent of 'eius' (Tertullian, or possibly the reckoning) is uncertain.

passages.original: Sed, quia apud omnes gentes instituta manent non fatorum ratione, quae ubique una est, sicut tractant, sed hominum excogitatione — quidquid enim alicui, qui primus putatus est apud suos, ratione dignum uisum est et aptum decori, statuit quibus praeerat —, inde una quaeque regio uel gens propria habet quae seruet, sicut Solon et Licurgus multa statuerant, quae a Graecis legis more seruarentur, quae paulatim deficiente regno eorum oblitterata sunt.
passages.english: But since among all nations institutions persist not by the reckoning of the fates, which is one and the same everywhere, as they argue, but by the devising of men (for whatever seemed reasonable and fitting for propriety to someone who was reckoned foremost among his own people, he established for those over whom he presided), it follows that each region or nation has its own [institutions] to observe, just as Solon and Lycurgus had established many things which were to be observed by the Greeks in the manner of law, and which, as their dominion gradually declined, were wiped out.
passages.notes: 'qui primus putatus est' may mean 'who was considered the first [lawgiver]' or 'who was held to be the chief' among his people; rendered as 'foremost'.
